title: Placental Insufficiency -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Placental insufficiency, also known as uteroplacental insufficiency, is a complex obstetric condition characterized by inadequate perfusion of the placenta, leading to suboptimal oxygen and nutrient delivery to the fetus. This condition is implicated in significant perinatal complications, including preeclampsia, fetal growth restriction, oligohydramnios, and stillbirth, and remains a major contributor to global perinatal morbidity and mortality. This course reviews the pathophysiology of placental insufficiency, which results from defective trophoblast invasion, incomplete spiral artery remodeling, and maternal or fetal factors such as hypertensive disorders, vascular disease, extremes of maternal age, obesity, or assisted reproductive technology. Participants will also gain an understanding of its clinical diagnosis, involving clinical suspicion that arises from abnormal fetal growth patterns, Doppler studies, and ultrasonographic findings. Advanced imaging modalities that show promise for early detection in high-risk pregnancies, timely interventions, including low-dose aspirin, targeted surveillance, and emerging therapies such as low-molecular-weight heparin, to mitigate adverse outcomes, are also reviewed.

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This course explores the underlying pathophysiologic mechanisms involved in pregnancies complicated by placental insufficiency and how they inform the interpretation of Doppler and imaging studies, early biomarkers, risk factors, and the application of individualized interventions. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance the learner's competence in identifying placental insufficiency, performing the recommended evaluation, and implementing an appropriate interprofessional approach to manage this condition, thereby improving patient-centered decision-making and ultimately supporting safer, more effective management of high-risk pregnancies.

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Continuing Education Activity

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Introduction
content: Placental insufficiency, also known as uteroplacental insufficiency, contributes to a broad spectrum of obstetric complications, including preeclampsia, fetal growth restriction (FGR), oligohydramnios, and stillbirth. This condition accounts for a substantial proportion of global perinatal morbidity and mortality. Despite extensive research, no universally accepted definition has been established. The disorder generally involves inadequate placental perfusion, which leads to insufficient delivery of oxygen and nutrients to the fetus. [1] [2]

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Introduction
content: Recent evidence underscores the lack of a pathognomonic clinical or histologic marker, creating challenges in achieving uniform diagnosis and study of placental insufficiency. [3] Current understanding characterizes the condition as a progressive decline in placental function that culminates in chronic fetal hypoxemia, metabolic acidosis, and FGR. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Fetal Growth Restriction ," for further information. Physiologically, hypoxemia triggers adaptive fetal responses, including redistribution of blood flow toward vital organs (brain sparing), diminished fetal movement, and reduced somatic growth. Histopathologic patterns commonly linked to placental insufficiency include distal villous hypoplasia, increased syncytial knots, maternal vascular malperfusion, placental infarctions, and fibrin deposition. [4] [5]

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Introduction
content: Advanced imaging modalities, including placental magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and 3-dimensional power Doppler, have demonstrated potential in quantifying abnormal placental morphology and perfusion. These technologies reveal findings, eg, reduced placental volume and altered vascular resistance. [6] [7] [8] Although not yet standard in clinical practice, such imaging may enable earlier detection of high-risk pregnancies in the future.

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Etiology
content: The pathogenesis of placental insufficiency is multifactorial and complex, involving both maternal and fetal components. The most commonly implicated maternal factors include hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (especially early-onset preeclampsia), preexisting vascular disease (eg, chronic hypertension, diabetes, or lupus), and environmental exposures, including tobacco, alcohol, or substance use. [9] Emerging research emphasizes the role of abnormal trophoblast invasion and defective remodeling of the spiral arteries during early placentation as key contributors to impaired uteroplacental perfusion. [10] Inadequate conversion of high-resistance uterine arteries into low-resistance vessels impairs maternal blood flow to the placenta and contributes to downstream fetal growth compromise. title: Placental Insufficiency -- Etiology
content: Extremes of maternal age (younger than 18 or older than 35 years) Primiparity Obesity or severe maternal malnutrition Assisted reproductive technology (ART) pregnancies Thrombophilia or antiphospholipid antibody syndrome Multiple gestation Use of certain medications (eg, antiepileptics, chemotherapeutics, and some anticoagulants) [11]

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Etiology
content: Early identification through screening with uterine artery Doppler studies in the first and early second trimesters can predict the risk of developing placental insufficiency, particularly in high-risk populations. [12] Abnormal findings, eg, persistent notching or elevated pulsatility index, are associated with a higher likelihood of subsequent FGR or preeclampsia.

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Epidemiology
content: Prematurity remains the leading global cause of neonatal death, followed closely by FGR, which affects approximately 5% to 8% of pregnancies worldwide. [1] Placental insufficiency is a key contributor to adverse outcomes, including FGR, preterm labor, preeclampsia, and stillbirth—conditions that together impact up to 15% of pregnancies. [3]

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Epidemiology
content: The risk of spontaneous preterm labor is more than 3 times higher in fetuses affected by FGR compared to their appropriately grown peers, and perinatal mortality is increased up to 6-fold in these cases. [4] Despite advancements in prenatal surveillance, nearly half of all FGR cases are not detected until after birth, underscoring the challenges in early recognition of placental dysfunction. [5]

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Pathophysiology
content: Placental insufficiency arises from disruptions in the maternal–fetal interface that impair the delivery of oxygen and nutrients. Central to this process is a failure in early gestational placentation, characterized by inadequate trophoblast invasion and incomplete spiral artery remodeling. [6] This leads to the persistence of high-resistance, low-flow uterine vessels, ultimately resulting in reduced uteroplacental perfusion. Abnormal umbilical artery Doppler flow, particularly elevated resistance or absent and reversed end-diastolic flow, reflects increased placental vascular resistance and correlates with the severity of fetal compromise. [7] Contributing structural abnormalities may include villous maldevelopment, infarction, or altered placental membrane insertion.

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Pathophysiology
content: Successful placental development relies on trophoblastic invasion of maternal vessels, mediated by matrix metalloproteinases and adhesion molecules secreted by cytotrophoblasts. [9] This process transforms the maternal spiral arteries into dilated, low-resistance conduits devoid of vasomotor control. Any disruption—genetic, inflammatory, vascular, or immune-mediated—can result in hypoperfusion, placental thrombosis, fibrin deposition, and infarction, all of which are pathologically associated with FGR. [10] Moreover, placental "globularity"—an increased thickness-to-volume ratio—has recently been proposed as a compensatory architectural change in response to insufficiency and may be identified via MRI or 3D ultrasound in high-risk pregnancies. [11]

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Pathophysiology
content: The placenta is a metabolically active organ that consumes up to 70% of available glucose and 40% of oxygen from the uterine circulation under physiologic conditions. [12] For optimal fetal growth, nutrient delivery must exceed placental metabolic demand. If this balance is disrupted, fetal nutrient availability declines. Additionally, placental lateralization, or asymmetric implantation, has been increasingly associated with impaired perfusion and persistent uterine artery notching, particularly when implantation favors one uterine side over another. This phenomenon has been correlated with increased risk for preeclampsia and relative placental insufficiency, especially in first pregnancies. [13]

title: Placental Insufficiency -- History and Physical -- Clinical Features
content: FGR is the most clinically recognized manifestation of placental insufficiency. Neonates may present preterm or small for gestational age (SGA), with body proportions reflecting the timing and severity of the growth restriction. Based on additional fetal biometric parameters, including head circumference, abdominal circumference, femur length, and biparietal diameter, FGR can be subcategorized into symmetrical and asymmetrical forms. In symmetrical FGR, all growth parameters are proportionally reduced, whereas in asymmetrical FGR, the abdominal circumference is classically reduced below the tenth percentile, while other measurements are relatively preserved and may be within normal limits. Symmetrical FGR often reflects early placental insufficiency or genetic syndromes, whereas asymmetric FGR typically reflects later-occurring placental compromise. [14] Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Fetal Growth Restriction ," for further information on symmetrical and asymmetrical FGR.

title: Placental Insufficiency -- History and Physical -- Clinical Features
content: Maternal fundal height measurement is a common screening method for SGA and FGR between 24 and 38 weeks of gestation, as the measured height in centimeters should roughly match the gestational age in weeks. Particularly at 32 to 34 weeks, this method has shown a sensitivity of 65% to 85% and a specificity of 96% for identifying FGR, though conditions such as maternal obesity and uterine leiomyomas can reduce the accuracy of fundal height measurements. [15] Clinical suspicion usually arises during the second or third trimester when serial fundal height measurements plateau or lag. Once FGR is suspected, serial growth scans, Doppler velocimetry, and biophysical profiles are recommended to assess fetal well-being and determine the timing of delivery. [16] Neonatal findings characteristic of FGR include a birthweight below the tenth percentile for weight, and the newborn typically appears emaciated with decreased muscle mass and subcutaneous fat at birth. Additionally, the fetal head may look disproportionately large or small. The facies and the umbilical cord may appear thin.

title: Placental Insufficiency -- History and Physical -- Clinical Features
content: Uterine artery Doppler in the second trimester, showing persistent notching or elevated resistance, is an early marker of poor placentation. Umbilical artery Doppler changes, eg, reduced, absent, or reversed end-diastolic flow, suggest advanced placental disease. Declining biophysical profile scores, including decreased fetal movement, tone, or a nonreactive fetal heart rate tracing, are late signs of fetal compromise and often warrant delivery.

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Evaluation -- Doppler Velocimetry Evaluation
content: Although no universally accepted diagnostic test for placental insufficiency exists, clinicians rely on the integration of clinical assessment, ultrasonographic evaluation, and Doppler studies as the diagnostic standard. The 4 principal Doppler studies utilized in this evaluation include:

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Evaluation -- Doppler Velocimetry Evaluation
content: Uterine artery Doppler : This modality assesses maternal vascular remodeling. Persistent diastolic notching and elevated resistance after 20 weeks suggest failed placentation. The sensitivity of uterine artery Doppler for predicting severe FGR or preeclampsia approaches 85% in high-risk groups. [17]
contents: Placental Insufficiency -- Evaluation -- Doppler Velocimetry Evaluation. Uterine artery Doppler : This modality assesses maternal vascular remodeling. Persistent diastolic notching and elevated resistance after 20 weeks suggest failed placentation. The sensitivity of uterine artery Doppler for predicting severe FGR or preeclampsia approaches 85% in high-risk groups. [17]

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Evaluation -- Doppler Velocimetry Evaluation
content: Umbilical artery Doppler : Studies have not shown this modality to be clinically valuable in fetuses with normal growth patterns, but umbilical artery Doppler studies can help differentiate a fetus with growth restriction from a genetically small fetus. Umbilical artery Doppler findings reflect the level of placental resistance. Normal progression shows increased diastolic flow as pregnancy advances. Persistent high resistance or reversal of end-diastolic flow is associated with high perinatal mortality and necessitates close surveillance or delivery, depending on gestational age. [7] [18]

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Evaluation -- Doppler Velocimetry Evaluation
content: Middle cerebral artery (MCA) Doppler : To increase oxygenation of the fetal brain, fetal blood flow is redistributed to the cerebral vessels at the expense of the fetal body. This redistribution is reflected in a reduced pulsatility index due to middle cerebral artery vasodilatation, which continues to decrease as hypoxemia becomes more severe. [19] A low pulsatility index and increased diastolic flow ("brain sparing") suggest centralization of blood flow and are associated with poorer outcomes when combined with abnormal umbilical artery findings. [20]

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Evaluation -- Doppler Velocimetry Evaluation
content: Ductus venosus Doppler : This Doppler study is a sensitive marker of fetal cardiovascular compromise. Absent or reversed a-wave flow in the ductus venosus has been associated with impending fetal demise in the setting of severe FGR and may guide delivery decisions. [21]

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Evaluation -- Magnetic Resonance Imaging Evaluation
content: Fetal MRI, while not routinely used in standard obstetric care, offers high-resolution soft tissue visualization and may detect placental abnormalities earlier in high-risk pregnancies. Loss of flow voids on T2-weighted imaging has been proposed as an early marker of decreased uteroplacental perfusion. [11] MRI may also identify hematomas, infarctions, or abnormal vascular patterns not evident on ultrasound.

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Evaluation -- Laboratory Biomarkers
content: Additionally, recent findings continue to support the clinical utility of mid-trimester biomarkers in identifying pregnancies at risk for placental insufficiency. A 2024 prospective cohort study demonstrated that low levels of PlGF and elevated sFlt-1/PlGF ratios between 24 and 28 weeks of gestation were significantly associated with subsequent development of small-for-gestational-age neonates, underscoring their predictive value in early detection efforts. [22]

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Treatment / Management
content: No curative therapy currently exists for placental insufficiency apart from delivery once fetal viability has been reached. Early intervention and targeted management strategies, however, can significantly improve outcomes in high-risk pregnancies. Low-dose aspirin (commonly 81 mg daily), when started before 16 weeks of gestation in high-risk individuals, has been shown to improve placental perfusion and reduce the incidence of preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction. Antioxidant therapies, including vitamins C and E, have been investigated for their theoretical potential to promote placental health, although current evidence remains inconclusive. [11]

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Treatment / Management
content: Emerging evidence also highlights the potential role of low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) as an adjunct therapy. Both in vitro and clinical studies suggest that heparin enhances placental angiogenesis, stimulates trophoblastic proliferation, and reduces inflammation and apoptosis. Mechanistically, LMWH augments the activity of angiogenic mediators such as angiopoietin-2, VEGF receptor-3, and leptin, while regulating key factors including TNF-alpha and tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases. [4] Despite encouraging results, its clinical application remains investigational and is generally limited to patients with thrombophilia or recurrent pregnancy loss.

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Treatment / Management
content: Doppler ultrasound screening among high-risk populations, particularly between 12 and 14 weeks, can detect bilateral uterine artery notching—an early indication of impaired placentation. In such cases, initiation of low-dose aspirin is recommended. Meta-analytic data indicate that early surveillance and timely intervention may lower perinatal mortality by approximately 38%. [14] [16] Delivery timing should be tailored according to clinical considerations, as interventions may not benefit some fetuses (eg, aneuploidy or congenital infections), or some patients may prefer not to deliver an extremely premature viable fetus. Individualized, interprofessional approaches are recommended, with antenatal surveillance to help determine delivery timing. If delivery is planned, FGR alone does not necessitate cesarean delivery; this decision should depend on other clinical factors. [15] [23]

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Distinguishing FGR from small-for-gestational-age is essential when evaluating suspected placental insufficiency. Generally, while both may present with fetal weights below the tenth percentile, FGR is typically pathologic, most commonly due to placental dysfunction, genetic anomalies, or intrauterine infections. Conversely, small-for-gestational-age neonates are constitutionally small but otherwise healthy.

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Historically, FGR has been defined by fetal size, typically using a reference standard of estimated fetal weight or abdominal circumference below the tenth percentile for gestational age. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) employs this criterion for FGR. However, some fetuses are constitutionally small in accordance with their genetic growth potential and are not growth-restricted, while other fetuses that are appropriate for gestational age but have not achieved their full growth potential are growth-restricted. [24]

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Adding to this confusion is the term SGA, which is often used synonymously with FGR. ACOG and several other professional societies use SGA to describe newborns with birth weight below the tenth percentile for their gestational age. In contrast, others, including the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO), use SGA as a preliminary diagnosis to characterize an estimated or birth weight below the tenth percentile. [23] However, most experts use the term SGA to describe neonatal size that may or may not be associated with an underlying pathologic etiology, whereas FGR is solely due to an antenatal pathologic condition. [15] [25] [26] [27] [28] Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Fetal Growth Restriction ," for further information on SGA neonates.

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Umbilical artery Doppler is instrumental in differentiating between the conditions. Abnormal Doppler findings, eg, elevated resistance or absent/reversed end-diastolic flow, are strongly indicative of FGR and placental insufficiency. [11] [17] Other differential considerations include preeclampsia, oligohydramnios, maternal malnutrition, and chronic systemic diseases (eg,  lupus or hypertension), all of which can impair uteroplacental blood flow.

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Prognosis
content: Survivors of FGR resulting from placental insufficiency face a markedly elevated risk of neurodevelopmental disorders, including cerebral palsy, seizure disorders, and cognitive delay. A longitudinal study demonstrated that children who exhibited abnormal umbilical artery Doppler flow velocities in utero scored lower on IQ assessments at 5 years of age compared to controls. [3]

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Prognosis
content: Mounting evidence also links placental insufficiency and FGR to an increased likelihood of developing adult-onset conditions, eg, coronary artery disease, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes. This association aligns with the “Developmental Origins of Health and Disease” (DOHaD) hypothesis, which proposes that adverse intrauterine environments contribute to long-term metabolic and cardiovascular risk. Improvement in perinatal outcomes depends heavily on prolonging gestation. Among fetuses between 24 and 28 weeks, each additional week of pregnancy raises survival rates without major complications by approximately 10% to 15%. [4]

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Complications
content: The most serious complication of placental insufficiency is fetal demise, especially when placentation fails entirely. For fetuses that survive, complications may include: Severe FGR and prematurity Metabolic derangements (eg, hypoglycemia, anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia) Neurologic injury, eg, hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, intraventricular hemorrhage (particularly with absent or reversed umbilical artery end-diastolic flow) [11] Multisystem compromise secondary to chronic hypoxemia; the fetus redistributes blood to vital organs (brain, heart) at the expense of others (kidneys, gastrointestinal tract), increasing risks of necrotizing colitis and renal dysfunction [10] [17] Many of these complications are directly related to the degree of placental resistance as visualized by Doppler studies.

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Prenatal care remains the cornerstone of prevention and early recognition. Although no intervention can fully prevent placental insufficiency, early detection through serial ultrasounds, Doppler assessments, and MRI (when indicated) allows for optimal monitoring and timely delivery planning.

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Patient education should emphasize the importance of antenatal visits, adherence to medical recommendations (eg, low-dose aspirin when indicated), and awareness of warning signs, eg, reduced fetal movements. Although therapies like heparin remain investigational, they may offer benefit in select high-risk populations.

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: No definitive cure for placental insufficiency has been identified; however, early detection, close surveillance, and interprofessional care can mitigate many of its consequences. A 2020 meta-analysis suggested that heparin therapy may promote fetal growth and prolong gestation in pregnancies complicated by placental insufficiency but does not significantly reduce neonatal morbidity. [4]

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Placental insufficiency, or uteroplacental insufficiency, results from inadequate perfusion of the placenta, leading to reduced oxygen and nutrient delivery to the fetus. This dysfunction contributes to complications such as FGR, preeclampsia, oligohydramnios, and stillbirth. Survivors of growth restriction face elevated risks of neurodevelopmental impairment, including cerebral palsy and cognitive delay, and later-life conditions such as coronary artery disease, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes. Early identification through Doppler studies, biomarkers, and imaging, along with preventive measures like low-dose aspirin, remains central to optimizing maternal and fetal outcomes.

title: Placental Insufficiency -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Interprofessional collaboration is critical in managing placental insufficiency. Physicians and advanced practitioners, including maternal-fetal medicine specialists and neonatologists, must interpret Doppler and imaging results, stratify risk, and coordinate individualized care plans, while providing continuous patient monitoring, education, and support. Nurses are essential in delivering hands-on care, performing routine assessments, ensuring patient compliance with medical recommendations, ongoing fetal monitoring, and patient education to support adherence and early recognition of complications. Pharmacists contribute by managing and advising on the safe use of medications, particularly when dealing with antenatal corticosteroids or other pharmacological interventions, while sonographers and radiologists contribute to accurate imaging assessment. Effective interprofessional communication is crucial for synchronizing efforts across the healthcare team, ensuring shared decision-making and coordinated follow-up, thereby strengthening patient safety, enhancing outcomes, and promoting high-functioning team performance in the management of high-risk pregnancies.
